se-europe-early-farmers.description: Farming reached southeastern Europe in the mid-7th millennium BCE with migrants whose ancestry was related to Anatolia's early farmers. From here farming groups took two paths: some passed through toward northern and western Europe, while others stayed and mixed extensively with hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are individuals associated with the Starčevo, Körös and Criș archaeological cultures, and their DNA shows how closely the region's early farmers resemble Anatolia's: Neolithic genomes from Bulgaria, Croatia, Macedonia, Serbia and Romania cluster tightly with those of early farmers from northwestern Anatolia. The movement behind that resemblance can be seen in single lives. At Lepenski Vir in the Iron Gates, where groups that differed in both ancestry and way of getting food met, two individuals dated 6200–5600 BCE carry only Anatolian-related ancestry, and isotope evidence suggests they were migrants.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Almost all of their ancestry came from Anatolian-related farmers. Modelled as a mix of Anatolian farmers and western hunter-gatherers (the foragers of western and central Europe), Balkan Neolithic genomes are about 98 percent Anatolian-related, leaving roughly one part in fifty to hunter-gatherers. In Hungary, most early Neolithic genomes are statistically indistinguishable from those of Neolithic Anatolians. Mixing did happen, but unevenly. One study finds about 8 percent hunter-gatherer ancestry in an early Starčevo individual from Hungary, gained only shortly before that person lived; another models eight of nine individuals from Malak Preslavets in Bulgaria, from the mid-6th millennium BCE, with about 15 percent western and 4 percent eastern hunter-gatherer ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The two paths left different marks. One study finds that in the north and west, later mixing with hunter-gatherers came disproportionately through men, while the groups that stayed in the southeast mixed without that bias. In Hungary, hunter-gatherer ancestry rose gradually through the Neolithic, and Balkan populations of the Copper Age carry significantly more of it than their Neolithic predecessors. That rise came at roughly the same time as a similar resurgence of hunter-gatherer ancestry in central Europe and Iberia.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: It is open whether two sources, Anatolian farmers and western hunter-gatherers, are enough to describe every Neolithic farmer in the region. One study finds five Neolithic individuals from the Peloponnese in southern Greece, from about 4000 BCE, and one from Bulgaria shifted toward the hunter-gatherers of the Caucasus and away from western hunter-gatherers, compared with other Anatolian and Balkan farmers. The pattern rests on just six genomes, but it hints that some communities had a further source of ancestry that the two-part model leaves out.

caveats: Individuals are grouped by the archaeological label in the source data (Starčevo, Körös, Criș, or early Neolithic Greece); several figures on this page come from studies of Balkan Neolithic farmers as a whole.

lbk-farmers.description: Farmers associated with the Linear Pottery culture (LBK), whose genomes show that early farmers in Germany carried only a small share of ancestry from the hunter-gatherers living around them. That share grew markedly among later farmers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The individuals here are grouped by their association with the Linear Pottery culture, abbreviated LBK from its German name, Linearbandkeramik. A 2015 study found that between 8,000 and 7,000 years ago, early farmers in Germany, Hungary and Spain were closely related to one another and distinct from the hunter-gatherers near them. One LBK-associated genome, from Stuttgart, serves in a 2014 study as the reference for early European farmers, one of three deeply different sources from which most present-day Europeans can be modelled.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their ancestry is overwhelmingly that of farmers related to Anatolia's, with only about 4–5 percent from hunter-gatherers, roughly one part in twenty. Mixed ancestry comes in stretches that shorten with every generation, which lets geneticists estimate when the mixing happened: for LBK farmers in Germany, about 5545 BCE, give or take 65 years. Looking much further back, the 2014 model assigns about 44 percent of the Stuttgart genome's ancestry, give or take 10, to 'Basal Eurasians', a lineage that split off before other non-African lineages diversified. No sampled individual belongs to that lineage; it is known only from the model.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Before them, the first farmers of northern and western Europe passed through southeastern Europe while mixing only a little with hunter-gatherers there. After them, hunter-gatherer ancestry returned. In Germany, the Middle Neolithic grouping carries about 17 percent, nearly four times the LBK share, and a second study finds the same rise among Middle Neolithic farmers in both Germany and Spain. Averages hide sharp local differences: at Blätterhöhle in Germany, where farmer and hunter-gatherer occupation overlapped until late, three Middle Neolithic individuals classed as farmers by isotope analysis carry 40–50 percent hunter-gatherer ancestry. One study finds that this later mixing in the north and west came disproportionately through men.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Which hunter-gatherers the LBK farmers mixed with is not settled. Their hunter-gatherer ancestry is closest to a combination of two sequenced Mesolithic (late hunter-gatherer) genomes, but the match is not statistically significant. The estimate also pools Stuttgart with LBK samples from farther northeast, such as Halberstadt, so differences between communities may be hidden.

caveats: Individuals are grouped by the LBK label in the source data, so the group pools sites and phases from across central Europe.

iberia-early-neolithic.description: Early farmers of the Iberian Peninsula, who carried mostly ancestry related to Anatolia's early farmers, with a smaller share from hunter-gatherers. Iberian Neolithic genomes also resemble those of Neolithic Britain, which suggests that farming travelled to Britain along the Mediterranean.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Iberia's early farmers were closely related to early farmers in Germany and Hungary, and distinct from local hunter-gatherers, in a 2015 study of people who lived between 8,000 and 7,000 years ago. Iberia's hunter-gatherers were themselves far from uniform: a 2019 study, which analyses 44 new Neolithic individuals from the peninsula, finds strong genetic differences between the northwest and the southeast before farming spread.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Some of the hunter-gatherer ancestry in Iberia's early farmers may have been acquired along their migration route. Mixed ancestry is inherited in stretches that shorten with every generation, so their length dates the mixing: 5650 BCE on average for Early Neolithic Iberians, give or take 65 years. Farming is thought to have begun in Spain around 5500 BCE, which is later than that date.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The hunter-gatherer share kept rising after the Early Neolithic, to about 23 percent in the Middle Neolithic and about 27 percent in the Chalcolithic (Copper Age), according to a 2017 study; a 2015 study sees the same rise in Spain and Germany. The link continues into the Copper Age: in Iberians associated with the Bell Beaker complex, a set of pottery and other material traditions, the farmer-related ancestry fits Iberia's own Middle Neolithic and Copper Age populations best, not central or northern European ones. Farmers from the continent are modelled as reaching Britain by 3975–3722 BCE (95 percent interval), and British Neolithic genomes resemble Irish and Iberian ones more than central European ones, which fits farming reaching Britain and Ireland along the Mediterranean route.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The mixing date shifts with the sample: using only the five oldest farmers moves it back to 5860 BCE. An estimate that moves like this leaves open how much hunter-gatherer ancestry arrived with the first farmers and how much was added in Iberia. The Mediterranean route to Britain is a similar kind of inference: genomes show that Iberian and British farmers resemble each other, not the path any of them took.

caveats: The group pools the source labels Spain_EN and Portugal_EN_Cardial, so it mixes sites across the peninsula.

britain-neolithic.description: The genomes of Britain's Neolithic farmers show that farming arrived around 4000 BCE overwhelmingly through the immigration of farmers from continental Europe, and not mainly through local hunter-gatherers adopting it. Their ancestry was mostly related to Anatolia's early farmers, with small hunter-gatherer contributions.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Whether Neolithic practices reached Britain with migrants or were taken up by the hunter-gatherers already living there is the question these genomes help to answer. A 2019 study put it to 67 Neolithic individuals from Britain, setting them beside six Mesolithic individuals, hunter-gatherers from the period before farming; all six cluster with western hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The earliest Neolithic individual in the study, from McArthur Cave in Scotland, dates to 3951–3780 BCE. The study models continental farmers as arriving in Britain by 3975–3722 BCE (a 95 percent interval), close to the time Neolithic practices appear there, around 4000 BCE. The Mesolithic and Neolithic individuals together span 8500–2500 BCE.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In the authors' model the Anatolian-farmer-related share averages about 74 percent, leaving about a quarter from western hunter-gatherers. The authors find only low levels of mixing with Britain's own hunter-gatherers, and no later resurgence of hunter-gatherer ancestry. The study finds the share uneven across Britain: lowest in Wales, higher in south-west and central England, and higher again in south-east England and Scotland. In south-east England the elevated level is older and was probably acquired on the continent, and only the individuals from Raschoille Cave show recent mixing, within about 10 generations.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The farmers resemble Irish and Iberian Neolithic genomes more than central European ones, which fits farming reaching Britain and Ireland along the Mediterranean route. None of the 51 Neolithic individuals in a 2018 study had any steppe affinity, and the mix of farmer and hunter-gatherer ancestry stayed stable for roughly a millennium and a half, until about 2450 BCE. Then migrants bringing Beaker traditions, a distinctive set of pottery and other material, added a third, steppe-related component. The arrival of the Beaker complex was associated with the replacement of about 90 percent of Britain's gene pool within a few hundred years.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The split between farmer and hunter-gatherer ancestry depends on the analysis: a 2022 study summarises earlier work as about 80 percent early-European-farmer and 20 percent western hunter-gatherer ancestry. Where the farmers' ancestors lived on the continent is not shown directly either. Resemblance to Iberian and Irish genomes points to a Mediterranean route, but a resemblance between genomes is not a record of a journey.

caveats: Figures quoted from the 2019 study describe its own 67 Neolithic individuals, not every individual shown on the map.
Individuals are grouped by the source labels Scotland_N, England_N, England_EN, England_EN_Megalithic and Wales_N, so the group pools sites and centuries from across Britain.

trypillia-farmers.description: Farming groups of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture, whose ancestry included only a little derived from the Caucasus and the lower Volga. The Usatove-associated people, by contrast, are modelled as a roughly equal mix of Trypillia-associated farmers and migrants related to that region.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: In the 2025 study's summary of earlier work, Cucuteni–Trypillia farming groups spread east across the Carpathians to the Dnipro Valley around 4800 BCE, with ancestry mainly derived from early European farmers plus some from western hunter-gatherers. The study adds a measurement: it samples 24 Trypillia individuals and models where their ancestry came from.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: For 23 of the 24 sampled individuals, a model with three sources fits: on average about 81 percent from farmers of the Balkan Eneolithic (Copper Age), about 14 percent from Balkan hunter-gatherers and about 5 percent from the Caucasus–Lower Volga (CLV) cline. A cline is a gradual change in ancestry across geography, here between the Caucasus and the lower Volga. The authors date the mixing of these sources to 4595 BCE, with a 95 percent interval of 4832–4358 BCE.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Trypillia-associated farmers contributed about 55 percent of the ancestry of the Usatove-associated people, who are modelled as mixing them with an intermediate group from the CLV cline that supplied about 45 percent. CLV ancestry did not enter every community alike: some of its carriers, as at Giurgiulesti and Csongrad, advanced to the Balkans and the Carpathian region largely without mixing with people on the way, while Usatove took in far more of it than Trypillia.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: How the Usatove mixing happened is untested. The authors suggest a trading outpost in the Danube–Dniester delta, a coexisting 'commonwealth' of cultures, or Trypillia farmers under dominance by CLV-related groups, and the DNA does not choose between them. One of the 24 sampled Trypillia individuals does not fit the three-source model, and the percentages are averages from a statistical model, not measurements of any one person.

caveats: Individuals are grouped by the Trypillia label in the source data, so the group describes people attributed to a culture, not one genetic population.
Of the 31 individuals shown, 29 come from one site, Verteba Cave, so the group reflects that site more than the culture as a whole.
Figures quoted come from the 2025 study's 24 sampled Trypillia individuals, not necessarily every individual shown on the map.

globular-amphora.description: Farmers associated with the Globular Amphora culture, whose genetic cluster can be modelled as the only source of the farmer-related ancestry in Corded Ware-associated individuals. In Bohemia, however, the Globular Amphora individuals who lived at or after the time Corded Ware appeared show no detectable steppe ancestry.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: In Bohemia, a 2021 study suggests, the Globular Amphora individuals were newcomers and not locals: the dates of their mixing with hunter-gatherers point to a nonlocal arrival from a region with more hunter-gatherer gene flow, meaning interbreeding, such as Poland.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their ancestry combined farmer ancestry with a substantial hunter-gatherer share. In Bohemia they carry the most hunter-gatherer-related ancestry among the groups there before Corded Ware: 25.7 percent, give or take 1.4. A 2019 study used Globular Amphora as a stand-in for the farmer-related ancestry of Yamnaya-associated groups, which later expanded into Europe, and noted that this source was itself a mixture of farmer ancestry and at least 20 percent western hunter-gatherer ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The farmer-related ancestry in Corded Ware-associated individuals can be modelled as coming exclusively from a Globular Amphora-associated cluster, and in every sampled European region it co-occurs with steppe-related ancestry. From this the authors of a 2024 study infer that steppe-related ancestry spread mostly through groups that had already mixed with Globular Amphora-related farmers, as Yamnaya-associated groups did before their expansion. They treat contact zones such as the forest-steppe northwest of the Black Sea, where Globular Amphora and Yamnaya groups exchanged cultural elements, as probably central to Corded Ware's formation. With Globular Amphora standing in for farmer ancestry, the 2019 study finds about 13 percent of it in Yamnaya from Samara and about 17 percent in Yamnaya from Ukraine or the Caucasus.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Bohemian samples cannot show where Globular Amphora-related farmers and steppe-related groups met. Their lack of steppe ancestry suggests little biological exchange from Corded Ware- and Yamnaya-related people into the Rivnac and Globular Amphora groups of Bohemia, while the contact zone the 2024 authors discuss lies northwest of the Black Sea. That contact was once read as cultural only, since earlier data from few individuals suggested no more than cultural influence. The farmer-related source is itself a stand-in: a 2015 model of Corded Ware-associated individuals from Germany used Middle Neolithic populations, where the 2024 study uses a Globular Amphora-associated cluster.

caveats: Individuals are grouped by their association with the Globular Amphora culture, so the group may include people of varied ancestry.
The source labels place 33 of the 39 individuals in Poland and 6 in Czechia, while the Bohemian figures quoted here come from a study of Bohemia.
